summary: A funny boxed-toy mock-up of a kid's drawing is a pleasant gift gag, but no source shows anyone paying $9 for it and Canva is free. It is also the third near-identical 'photo to funny keepsake bundle' idea in the pipeline (alterpaw, giftlet), with no distribution edge.

demand.evidence: RESEARCH.md shows the category pays ($99 Budsies, $75 Artkive, £18-£20 keyrings) but admits 'no source shows people paying $9 for it specifically' and has no sales data for the mock-up niche. Reddit/blog sources only show parents have too many drawings. Nobody is described as upset if it vanished.

statusQuo.evidence: Status quo is photograph-and-toss, or free Canva/mockup templates (Etsy PSDs at $1.49-$4.24). That is a real workaround but a cheap, painless one; the research itself says 'parents rarely do it', which reads as low pain, not unmet pain.

specificity.evidence: Target is 'parents and grandparents' gifting a drawing the week before a holiday. That is a plausible moment but a category, not a named person; there is no quote or conversation behind it. Consequence of not solving it is a mild missed gag.

wedge.evidence: Narrow and weekend-buildable: one photo, one toy-box template, watermarked preview, $9 to unwatermark. Genuinely cheap to test. Weakness is that the wedge is one-time and seasonal, with no retention.

futureFit.evidence: Generic image tools and chat assistants will make 'turn this drawing into a toy box' a one-prompt task for free within the 3-year window, which makes a $9 template product less essential, not more. Moat is taste and templates, which are easy to copy (RESEARCH.md).

premises: A $9 instant digital option fills a gap between free DIY and $18-$100 physical keepsakes. Research confirms the gap on price but not that anyone wants to buy in it.
Grandparents and relatives will buy a finished mock-up image rather than make or skip it. Unsupported: no evidence of purchase behaviour at this price.
Parents will upload photos of their children's art to a new site. Plausible with a delete-after-7-days policy, but trust and COPPA framing add friction.
The product is distinct from alterpaw and giftlet. Weak: same buyer motive (funny personalised gift from a photo), same price band, same channels.
alternatives: Minimal: skip the app. Make a single Canva or static page with 3 sample toy boxes from a stock kid-drawing, put a $9 Stripe link and 'send me the drawing, I'll send it back in 24h' on it, and hand-make the first 5 orders. Tests willingness to pay in a weekend with no pipeline.

Extend an existing repo: add a 'kid's drawing as toy box' template to alterpaw (photo to funny bundle, $9-$20) instead of a separate product. Reuses upload, compositing, copy generation and payment, and shares the same audience and channels.
Lateral: sell it as a Q4 gift-season template pack for designers and Etsy sellers rather than to parents. Etsy mockups already sell at $1.49-$4.24, which shows the price ceiling is low.
wedge: One upload, one toy-box template, watermarked preview, $9 to remove the watermark. Better still, a fake-door page with sample outputs and a $9 button, measuring clicks before any code.

feasibility.notes: M1 is buildable in a weekend: Next.js on Cloudflare Workers (OpenNext), client-side @imgly/background-removal, canvas compositing of one template, free-model blurb, R2 with a 7-day lifecycle. Watch the 3 MiB Worker bundle limit against background-removal assets (run it in the browser, not the Worker). The one test that proves M1: POST /api/preview with a 1200x1600 JPG returns a watermarked PNG in under 30 seconds, and a blank page returns 422. Payment arrives in M2, so M1 proves only the render, not demand.

risks: Willingness to pay $9 versus free Canva and DIY is unproven.
One-time, seasonal purchase (Nov-Dec peak) with no retention. Today is 2026-11-18, so a two-week test lands in the peak but a build would not be live in time to catch much of it.
Photos of children: privacy, consent, COPPA framing, and a stronger trust bar than a pet photo.
Heavy overlap with alterpaw and giftlet splits David's attention and channel effort across near-identical gift products, none of which has shown paid demand.
Trademark risk if templates drift toward real toy or cereal brands.
Easy to copy; no distribution advantage is identified (Pinterest and parent communities are crowded and hostile to promotion).
killCriteria: Not applicable to a pass. If David overrides: drop it if a fake-door page with sample outputs gets under 50 targeted visitors in 14 days with fewer than 5 email signups, or if fewer than 3 of the first 20 people shown a real preview click a $9 buy button.
m1Observation: Watch 5 parents or grandparents upload a drawing with no help: do they photograph it well enough for background removal, do they edit the blurb or accept it, do they share the watermarked preview, and do they hesitate or abandon at the $9 step. Note whether they compare it with Canva out loud.
